entries.title: Stationarity of the patch optimizer
entries.claims: To build the small-patch subspaces, the paper minimizes the norm of an ordered product of regional filters. From the first-order conditions at the minimizer it derives that each regional output state is dominated by its optimal density plus a small shift, ρ_j ≤ x_j + b·1.
entries.found: QICLean proves the consequences of this inequality. The regulator is bounded by b·1 and by ρ, its trace by b·rank Q + tr((1−Q)ρ) for every projection Q, and hence by 1/4 at the paper's starting radius. QICLean #607 recovers commutation from shifted powers. The inequality itself, and the commutation of the minimizing densities with the outputs, are not yet derived for the ordered objective. Until they are, Proposition 4.1 is not formalized.
entries.impact: No problem with the paper has been found. This is the most delicate open step in Proposition 4.1, because the paper reaches the inequality through descending trace calculations on a noncommutative objective. The note warns against substituting a simpler separable objective.
entries.plan: Carry out the descending trace calculations for the ordered objective, derive the commutation and first-order conditions, and apply the regulator bounds already proved.

entries.title: Birth, death and exchange as allowed operations
entries.claims: Handing a region from one party to another (birth or death), or swapping ownership between two copies of the state (exchange), costs reference error at most L^−30 (4L^−30 for the exchange), provided the region shares information at most L^−60 with its surroundings. Each move involves only the named parties.
entries.found: Both lemmas are proved with exactly the paper's hypotheses, including the canonical maps, their contractivity and both error bounds. On the party model built in #8843, with the registers of each region held by one party grouped into one register, the birth is proved to be a private map, one shared state and a private map, and the death the same with one shared effect. The exchange corrections are proved to be one private map on such grouped registers. The paper has one register per site, and the grouped registers are not yet identified with the registers of a frame. Also unstated is that the exchange's renaming is a reordering of registers. It is proved to keep every register with its party, but writing it as a reordering needs the same list with one register per site and per tag.
entries.impact: No problem with the paper has been found. What remains is to place the grouped monomials on the registers of a frame and to restate the renaming step of the exchange.
entries.plan: List the registers of a frame one per site and per tag, identified with the canonical coordinates. Move and group the registers of each region by reorderings and private unitaries, so that the birth, death and correction monomials act on that list, and write the exchange's renaming as a reordering of it.

entries.title: Rewriting a small patch as allowed operations
entries.claims: Lemma 6.3 rewrites the state near a small patch where ownership changes. It states that (1) the rewrite map is a contraction that moves the old reference state close to the new one, and (2) up to error L^−a the map is a polynomial sum of operations that the compression theorem allows.
entries.found: Part (1) is proved with exactly the paper's hypotheses. For part (2), Lean proves the branch expansion, the owner bookkeeping, the network of each branch with no wire from a vertex to itself, its truncation by Lemma 6.2 with error 2m/√k and at most k^(2m) terms independent of the site dimensions, and the final rescaling: for every δ > 0 there is a contraction within δ of the rewrite that is a sum of explicit product terms. Two steps are not yet formalized. Each product term is not yet written as an allowed monomial of Theorem 5.2, because the frame's registers have no layout by owner with one register per site and per tag. The term count is not yet polynomial in L, because the patches do not carry the bound on the number of cylinder terms from Proposition 4.1.
entries.impact: No problem with the paper has been found. What remains is the register layout of a frame and carrying the cylinder-term bound of Proposition 4.1 into the patch data.
entries.plan: List the frame's registers one per site and per tag, identified with the canonical coordinates, and read each product term as an allowed party chain with the front-register calculus already used for Lemmas 6.5 and 6.6. Carry the bound on the number of cylinder terms from Proposition 4.1, with bounded numbers of patches and affected holes, to make the count of terms polynomial in L.

entries.title: Clearance during the dyadic repainting
entries.claims: When a dyadic square changes owner, each elementary move keeps a clearance proportional to the distance from a few marked points, with one universal constant a₀.
entries.found: Lean first proved the clearance with a₀ = 1/5000 for any guides with the properties the paper's proof uses. #8910 builds the schedule of guides, derives those properties from the disjointness of the bands, and proves Lemma 7.2 for every square of the hierarchy with no added hypothesis. Formal guides are labellings of the plane that represent the paper's open chambers, and the estimates are proved for the labellings the schedule specifies. At the start of each edge and at the end of each repainting the schedule passes to a labelling that agrees with the one reached only off a few curves; no lattice site lies on those curves, so the labels at the sites are unchanged, matching the paper's sampling convention. On an interface curve the formal words take the label on one fixed side, while the paper's displacement takes the other side along two edges of each square. #8935 proves that the estimates, which are stated for closures, hold on all four edges for every guide read after one small displacement, and that such readings of the schedule's guides exist for every displacement. That the paper's sampled guides are these readings rests on the identification of the paper's open chambers with the formal labellings off a locally finite family of segments and on the genericity of the displacement, neither of which is formalized.
entries.impact: No problem with the paper. The clearance estimates of Lemma 7.2 are proved for every reading of the schedule's guides after a small displacement (#8910, #8935). Lemma 7.2 for the paper's chamber-sampled guides is established only conditionally: identifying those guides with the readings needs two facts not yet proved (the chambers are the open sets where the formal labellings are constant, off a locally finite family of segments, and the generic displacement is parallel to none of these segments).
entries.plan: Prove the two identification facts: describe the paper's open chambers as the constancy sets of the formal labellings off a locally finite family of segments, and show a generic displacement is parallel to none of them, so each sampled guide equals a reading. The protocol of Proposition 7.1 is separate work.

entries.title: Who owns the replacement of a shared resource
entries.claims: Lemma 5.1 removes a two-party shared state by replacing it with a stack of m fresh copies, at error r/√m. It also states that the replacement uses only operations local to the two parties plus normalized shared states, and that all shared states between the same two parties can be merged into one.
entries.found: The first Lean model had no notion of a party, so the locality clauses could not be stated (#8791). #8843 added parties and proved those clauses. #8853 proves the merging clause. Each freshly prepared shared state can be moved to the front, and the states between the same two parties combine into one normalized state. No hypotheses were added.
entries.impact: None. Lemma 5.1 is formalized as stated once #8853 merges.
entries.plan: Merge #8853. The aggregate map per party used by Theorem 5.2 is separate work.
